author: William Saville
reader_character: Jasper — adult first-person protagonist, externally they/them
title: The Keeper's Refusal
subtitle: Lanternweald — sixth expansion pass
content:
Neri told us the truth without looking at either of us.

They sat in the archive's west room, where the burned ledger rested under protective cloth. The door was closed, but not locked. Severus had offered to stay and had accepted Neri's request that he wait outside.

It was the first time Neri had asked me to hear something without calling it a meeting.

Maui sat beside me. He'd come because I wanted company, not because the old keepers belonged to his legend.

Neri folded their hands.

"I watched someone turn a traveler away during the Closed Bells," they said.

The room seemed to tighten.

"How old were you?" I asked.

"Old enough to understand the words. Young enough to believe an official would know better than I did."

They looked at the ledger.

"The keeper said the channels were unstable. He said opening the door might endanger everyone. A woman wanted to leave for her homeworld. She had family waiting. She begged him to let her pass."

"Did he?" Maui asked.

"No."

I heard the sea outside, impossibly distant from Moonroot Archive.

"What happened to her?" I asked.

"I don't know."

Neri's voice broke on the last word.

They took a breath.

"The keeper ordered the arch sealed. He used the language of safety and protection. He spoke as if refusing her was an act of compassion. I stood there and did nothing."

Maui's hand tightened on his knee.

I wanted to say that Neri had been a child, that they hadn't been responsible, that remembering was enough. But the woman had still been turned away. Her family had still waited on the other side.

"I don't know what you could have done then," I said. "I do know what you can do now."

Neri looked up.

"Tell the truth in the record," I said. "Help us change the rules that allowed it. And don't ask the people affected to make you feel forgiven."

They looked as though I had struck them.

"I wasn't going to—"

"I know," I said softly. "But I think you've been carrying this alone because you wanted a version where your silence made sense."

They stared at the table.

"Yes."

The word was almost inaudible.

We stayed a while. I asked what Neri remembered about the keeper's instructions, the weather, and the public notice. I did not ask for a name Neri had already said they couldn't reliably provide. Their memory could be a witness to an action without being proof of the scratched signature in the ledger.

Maui listened.

At one point Neri said, "I thought he was trying to keep us safe."

Maui shifted in his chair.

"I've told people I was protecting them," he said. "Sometimes I was. Sometimes I was just frightened of being blamed if something went wrong."

Neri looked at him.

"What did you do?"

"Things I regret."

He didn't turn the answer into a story about his greatness.

Later, Severus returned and asked whether Neri wanted their account documented as a signed statement, an anonymous summary, or kept private while they considered it. They chose a signed statement with restricted access until the wording could be reviewed.

Orin prepared the form.

I stood beside Neri while they read it.

The final paragraph did not identify the keeper by name. It recorded what Neri had witnessed: a traveler requesting departure, an official refusing it, and a claimed safety reason that had not been documented with an alternative plan.

Neri signed.

Then they put down the pen and wept.

I did not know whether to embrace them. I asked.

They nodded.

I held them for a moment, feeling how thin their shoulders were beneath the old coat. My own throat hurt. I wanted the world to be the kind of place where admitting wrong made the consequence disappear.

It wasn't.

At the next council session, Neri gave permission to read the verified portion of their testimony. The room listened. A woman in the audience asked whether other witnesses could be contacted without being pressured to relive what had happened.

"Yes," Neri said. "And they may refuse."

Someone asked whether the old keeper had meant well.

I could feel the room searching for an easier ending.

I stood.

"Intention matters to understanding how decisions were made," I said. "It doesn't make a locked exit harmless. A person who wasn't allowed to leave was still denied a choice."

The council approved a review of every emergency crossing procedure. Volunteers would be trained to explain safe options and record only the information necessary to help. The lower service passage would stay closed until the structural team could inspect it; closure of an unsafe maintenance tunnel would never be used to justify blocking the independent traveler Threadways.

That distinction took an entire afternoon to write correctly.

Afterward, Maui and I walked to the cove.

"I wanted to shout," he admitted.

"I know."

"You didn't."

"I wanted to."

He looked at me.

"Why didn't you?"

"Because Neri wasn't asking me to make them feel good. They were trying to say something difficult. I wanted to hear it without turning their shame into my performance."

Maui nodded.

The light had grown gold over the sea-glass orchard. I could smell wet earth and the faint spice of rosemary. The little bench stood empty.

We sat.

"I was wrong about many things," Maui said. "Still am, probably."

"Very probably."

He smiled.

I leaned against him.

"Do you think Neri's testimony will help?" he asked.

"Yes. Not because it ends the question. Because people can now ask better questions."

He put his hand over mine.

We watched a boat make the safe turn toward the upper landing, its lantern moving steadily through the evening light.

The harbor did not become innocent because somebody had spoken.

But the words were out in the open.

That mattered.
